positions.standard_position: All disputes arising out of or in connection with the Agreement must be referred exclusively to binding institutional arbitration before a single arbitrator — SIAC/Singapore/English on Amperesand Pte Ltd (SG) paper, and AAA Commercial Arbitration Rules seated in Nevada on Amperesand Inc (US) paper (mNDA 4.7 Clause 16) — with a court carve-out limited to injunctive/equitable relief. (A Delaware seat appears frequently in executed US deals but is observed drift, not the template standard; see acceptable_fallbacks.)
positions.rationale: Arbitration is core to Amperesand's NDA risk posture: as a Singapore-incorporated group with a US entity, arbitration delivers (1) confidentiality of proceedings (critical when the dispute itself concerns trade secrets/confidential information), (2) cross-border enforceability of awards under the New York Convention against counterparties in the EU, Asia, Korea, and the US where a domestic court judgment would be far harder to enforce, and (3) a single neutral forum with a sole arbitrator that keeps NDA-scale disputes fast and cost-efficient. Losing arbitration to court litigation forfeits all three benefits and frequently places Amperesand in the counterparty's home courts. The forum, seat, institution, number of arbitrators, and any fee-shifting all materially affect cost and outcome, so this clause is a genuine commercial-risk item rather than pure boilerplate — but it is rarely a standalone dealbreaker on an NDA, so it sits in the mid-range.

acceptable_fallbacks.position: US-paper AAA arbitration, single arbitrator, but seated in Delaware rather than the template's Nevada seat (seat drift, typically to align with Delaware governing law). The most common observed US-paper deviation; institution, rules, and sole-arbitrator structure all preserved.

SIAC/Singapore/English single-arbitrator arbitration applied to a non-SG counterparty — i.e., SG paper used cross-border instead of US AAA. Forum is Amperesand's own preferred SIAC, so favorable to Amperesand; only downside is potential added friction enforcing an SIAC award against a US-domiciled entity.
SIAC arbitration with a three-arbitrator tribunal (rather than sole arbitrator). Seat/rules/language remain standard SIAC; only the panel size and cost increase.
Arbitration before a reputable US institution other than AAA, using single-arbitrator or streamlined rules (e.g., JAMS Streamlined Rules or ICDR Commercial Rules).

Arbitration with a pre-arbitration escalation/cooling-off step (good-faith senior-management negotiation or optional mediation) before AAA/SIAC arbitration. Adds a procedural gate but preserves arbitration as the binding forum.
AAA arbitration with a counterparty-home seat in a US city plus minor add-ons (punitive-damages exclusion, each-party-bears-own-fees). Institution standard; seat is a concession.

Court litigation in lieu of arbitration on counterparty paper (no arbitration clause), where the named forum is a defined neutral or US-nexus court — accepted in practice with meaningful but tolerable downside (loss of confidentiality/finality).

walk_away_triggers: No dispute-resolution mechanism at all — governing-law clause only, leaving forum and process undefined (forces a jurisdiction fight and default litigation). Refuse: insert at minimum a defined forum.

Internally contradictory or unenforceable forum clause naming two incompatible institutions or seats in the same provision (e.g., a US arbitration institution combined with SIAC Singapore in one clause). Risk of a void clause and litigation over the clause itself. Always fix before signing.

Litigation (no arbitration) in the counterparty's home courts of an adverse or hard-to-enforce jurisdiction, especially with prevailing-party fee-shifting to the counterparty — strips confidentiality, neutrality, and adds asymmetric cost exposure.

Arbitration moved to the counterparty's home-jurisdiction seat under that counterparty's preferred institution where Amperesand has no nexus: examples include European or Asian institutional arbitration seats (e.g., ICC in Western Europe; KCAB or ICC in an Asian counterparty's home city). Resist; counter to SIAC Singapore (or neutral SIAC/ICC Singapore).

Prevailing-party attorneys'-fee-shifting bolted onto the dispute clause (not in Amperesand's template) — creates asymmetric downside if Amperesand is the responding/losing party. Push to delete or make each party bear own fees.

US-style jury-trial waiver inserted where it signals an intent to default to US court litigation rather than arbitration — acceptable as harmless surplusage alongside arbitration, but a red flag when paired with a litigation-only clause.

positions.standard_position: Neither Party may assign rights or delegate obligations without the other Party's prior written consent, except that (i) the Disclosing Party may assign to an acquirer of substantially all of its assets by operation of law and, in unilateral NDAs, also to any Affiliate, and (ii) in mutual NDAs Amperesand (Party A) may assign to any Affiliate on prior written notice only (no consent required); any purported assignment in violation is null and void, and assignment does not relieve the assignor of its obligations.
positions.rationale: Assignment controls who ultimately holds Amperesand's confidential information and who can transfer it. Amperesand's templates deliberately build in an asymmetry that favors Amperesand: in mutual NDAs Amperesand alone may assign to Affiliates on notice (preserving its internal corporate-restructuring and group-operational flexibility) while the counterparty must obtain consent; in unilateral NDAs (where Amperesand is the sole Disclosing Party) the M&A and Affiliate carve-outs run only to Amperesand. This protects Amperesand's M&A exit and group reorganization flexibility while ensuring it retains a veto over the counterparty transferring access to Amperesand's secrets to an unknown or competing third party. Reviewer flags noting one-sidedness that benefits Amperesand are not genuine risks to Amperesand — they reflect asymmetry that counterparties have accepted. The real risks are the inverse: counterparty paper that permits free or automatic assignment without consent, restricts only the Recipient (leaving the Discloser free to transfer in a mutual NDA), or grants the counterparty (not Amperesand) the unilateral carve-out. Because broad or free assignment lets a counterparty hand Amperesand's information to a competitor or unknown acquirer without approval, this is a high-weight clause.

acceptable_fallbacks.position: Consent requirement qualified by 'not to be unreasonably withheld (or delayed)' — mutual and balanced.

Mutual consent with a reciprocal M&A/change-of-control carve-out for either party (assignment without consent on merger, acquisition, or sale of substantially all assets, typically with successor assuming obligations).
Mutual consent with a reciprocal Affiliate assignment carve-out (either party may assign to an Affiliate, on notice or without consent).
Change-of-control / M&A assignment carve-out granted to Amperesand only (no equivalent for counterparty) — Amperesand-favorable.
Plain mutual prior-written-consent restriction with no carve-outs (matches conservative baseline); purported assignment void; assignment does not relieve obligations.
M&A/asset-acquisition carve-out conditioned on the acquirer/surviving entity not being a competitor (mutual non-competitor guard).

walk_away_triggers: Agreement freely binding on 'successors and assigns' with no consent or notice requirement, allowing either party to assign automatically (e.g., on a counterparty's acquisition or merger), transferring access to Amperesand's confidential information to an unknown third party.

Counterparty (not Amperesand) granted the unilateral right to assign to its affiliates or subsidiaries freely or in M&A without consent, while Amperesand needs the counterparty's consent — the asymmetry running against Amperesand.
In a mutual NDA, the assignment restriction is framed only against the 'Recipient,' leaving the Discloser (either party) free to assign its rights without consent.

M&A/change-of-control carve-out with a one-sided non-competitor restriction that applies only to Amperesand's acquirer (so a competitor acquiring Amperesand needs consent, but no equivalent constraint on the counterparty's acquirer).
No assignment clause at all, leaving assignment governed by permissive local-law defaults that could let the counterparty assign without Amperesand's consent.
Counterparty may freely assign to affiliates or subsidiaries without restriction while Amperesand may not assign without the counterparty's consent.

positions.standard_position: Amperesand's templates contain NO standalone non-solicitation covenant and no non-use/non-diversion covenant; an NDA is a confidentiality instrument, not a trade-restraint vehicle. An inserted non-solicit is treated as a prohibited, high-severity, walk-away clause. (A narrow, use-tethered, mutual non-solicit may be entertained only as a documented fallback on counterparty paper — see acceptable_fallbacks — not as Amperesand-standard language.)
positions.rationale: Amperesand treats an NDA as a confidentiality instrument, not an employment- or trade-restraint vehicle. A standalone non-solicit imports a substantive restrictive covenant (enforceability varies sharply by jurisdiction — US Delaware-law vs. Singapore-law/SIAC templates differ on reasonableness and consideration), constrains Amperesand's own hiring and business-development freedom, and is asymmetric where Amperesand is the smaller/receiving party. The playbook explicitly classifies an inserted non-solicit as a prohibited, high-severity, walk-away clause; permitting only the use-tethered non-diversion language keeps the restraint narrow, mutual in effect, and defensible while still protecting against misuse of Confidential Information to poach staff or customers.

acceptable_fallbacks.position: Mutual, narrowly targeted non-solicitation limited to personnel introduced in connection with the Purpose, capped at twelve (12) months, with an express general-advertising / non-targeted-recruiting carve-out — documented as an acceptable fallback (accepted with friction, medium severity), NOT a clean position.

A narrow, use-tethered mutual non-diversion formulation (tying any restraint to misuse of Confidential Information, capped at 1-2 years, with a general-advertising / non-targeted-recruiting carve-out), accepted only on counterparty paper as a low-risk term concession — NOT Amperesand-standard language.

walk_away_triggers: Any standalone non-solicitation covenant untethered from use of Confidential Information (playbook-prohibited; rated high)
Non-solicit period exceeding 12 months, or with no fixed term / perpetual restraint
Unilateral / one-way non-solicit binding only Amperesand
Non-solicit lacking a general-advertising and non-targeted-recruiting carve-out (capturing responses to public job postings)
Customer/supplier non-solicit broad enough to restrain ordinary business (a de facto non-compete)
Any accompanying non-competition covenant (separately playbook-prohibited and a walk-away trigger)
Liquidated-damages or indemnity tied to a non-solicit breach

positions.standard_position: Amperesand's NDA templates contain no non-competition clause, and an NDA should remain a confidentiality instrument only; Amperesand's preferred position is to include no non-compete, no non-compete-taint restriction, and no non-compete waiver in either direction.

acceptable_fallbacks.position: On Amperesand's own uNDA paper, a reciprocity-neutral, narrowly framed investing carve-out confirming a VC/investor Recipient may invest in or participate in other enterprises (including competitors), provided it is paired with confidentiality and no-use protections and ideally drafted as mutual/non-prejudicial language. Tolerated only for genuine VC/investor counterparties on Amperesand paper.

walk_away_triggers: One-sided non-compete-taint or 'residual contamination' restriction imposed only on Amperesand that bars Amperesand personnel exposed to a counterparty's Confidential Information from working on competing technology, including for internal use — a de facto non-compete on Amperesand's engineering teams and a dealbreaker-class concession.
Broad definition of 'competes' (same/similar functionality usable as an alternative) tied to a personnel-segregation or taint obligation, which can sterilize Amperesand's own R&D roadmap.

Non-compete waiver extracted from Amperesand as disclosing party requiring Amperesand to acknowledge that a counterparty (such as a large VC fund or investor) may invest in, consult for, or service Amperesand competitors, with no reciprocal protection and explicit non-interference language, on counterparty paper without offsetting confidentiality/use safeguards.
Any asymmetric non-compete obligation binding only Amperesand while leaving the counterparty unrestricted in a mutual (mNDA) context.
Any actual non-compete (restraint on Amperesand competing or soliciting) embedded in an NDA.
positions.rationale: Non-competition terms are dealbreaker-class because they can restrain Amperesand's core business and R&D far beyond the confidentiality purpose of an NDA. The executed set shows the real risk is not a classic non-compete but two recurring one-sided structures: (1) investor/advisor non-compete waivers that strip Amperesand of any reciprocal protection, extracted on counterparty paper without offsetting confidentiality or use safeguards; and (2) non-compete-taint clauses that quarantine Amperesand engineers who touch a counterparty's Confidential Information from building competing technology — even internally — effectively contaminating Amperesand's own development program. Both structures transfer disproportionate value to the counterparty and, in the mutual NDA context, are asymmetric. Accepting them can foreclose product lines, complicate clean-room defenses, and create breach exposure from ordinary internal engineering work. The only tolerable variant observed is a reciprocity-neutral VC investing carve-out on Amperesand's own paper.

Legal to set firm policy on whether investor/advisor non-compete waivers are ever acceptable on counterparty paper versus only on Amperesand paper.

positions.standard_position: Amperesand's standard NDAs contain NO indemnification, hold-harmless, or fee-shifting provision; confidentiality breaches are remedied through general-law damages and equitable relief, so the preferred position is to strike any indemnity or attorneys'-fees clause entirely.
positions.rationale: An NDA is an information-protection instrument, not a commercial risk-transfer contract, and injecting an indemnity converts an otherwise low-risk confidentiality exchange into open-ended, often uncapped financial liability. Every indemnity observed in the signed set is one-sided against the Recipient (seen in provisions from large infrastructure counterparties and engineering/fabrication counterparties) or creates exposure on Amperesand as Discloser, and several reach indemnity-basis or solicitor-client legal costs that far exceed party-and-party recovery and the actual loss. Because these are mutual NDAs, Amperesand is simultaneously Recipient and Discloser, so any Recipient-favouring indemnity is a live exposure whenever Amperesand receives information. Indemnities and fee-shifting also chill legitimate enforcement and broaden liability to cover "attempted or threatened" disclosure and to long affiliate/agent indemnitee lists. The rubric expressly treats indemnity in an NDA as dealbreaker-class, making this the highest-stakes clause category in the playbook.

acceptable_fallbacks.position: Mutual, reciprocal attorneys'-fees / costs-of-enforcement shifting where the breaching (non-prevailing) party pays the non-breaching party's reasonable fees — acceptable only because it is bilateral and limited to reasonable fees.

Narrow, scope-limited cost-indemnity running from Discloser to Recipient solely for costs reasonably incurred when the Discloser instructs the Recipient to pursue claims against a breaching representative or permitted recipient — tolerable because it is reciprocal in effect and capped to costs of instructed enforcement rather than general breach liability.

Broad one-way Recipient indemnity for all losses, damages, and costs (including legal costs on an indemnity basis) arising from breach — signed under commercial necessity with large counterparties only as a last-resort concession; treat as the outer boundary of what has been accepted, never a target, and only with mutual/capped pushback attempted first.

walk_away_triggers: Uncapped, one-way indemnity running only against the Recipient for any breach; if unavoidable, demand it be made mutual and subject to a liability cap and exclusion of indirect/consequential loss.
Legal/attorneys' costs recoverable on a solicitor-client or 'indemnity basis' rather than reasonable party-and-party costs.
Indemnity or liability extending to 'attempted or threatened' disclosure/violation and to a broad list of affiliates, agents, advisors, shareholders, officers, and directors as indemnitees.
Uncapped explicit damages liability for unauthorized use/disclosure with no limitation of liability.
Any non-mutual fee-shifting or indemnity that runs only in the counterparty's favour.
Indemnity lacking carve-outs aligned to the confidentiality exclusions (compelled disclosure, independently developed information, publicly available information).
counsel_must_confirm: No Amperesand template variants were supplied; the no-indemnity baseline is inferred from the deviation notes rather than verified against template text — confirm against the actual templates.

positions.standard_position: Notices effective on delivery by hand, email, or certified/registered mail to specified addresses; clean boilerplate (no-waiver, severability, entire agreement/merger, written-signed amendments, counterparts, PDF/e-signature execution) with the e-signature statutory reference matched to governing law (ESIGN + Delaware UETA on US/Delaware paper; Electronic Transactions Act 2010 on Singapore paper) and no extra regulatory obligations.
positions.rationale: This is administrative/boilerplate plumbing, but it is the operational backbone of the NDA: the notices block governs whether a demand, breach notice, or termination is validly served, and the entire-agreement/amendment-in-writing and counterparts/e-signature clauses determine enforceability and execution. The dominant real-world risk is not negotiation pressure on substance but template hygiene — Amperesand's Singapore-origin template has repeatedly been deployed on Delaware/US-governed deals while retaining Singapore statutory references, creating an internal governing-law conflict. A bare electronic-transactions-act-only artifact is cosmetically harmless (US e-signatures stand under the applicable US federal and state statutes regardless), but the bundled multi-statute residue is a recurring high-significance defect. The second risk is counterparties bolting on substantive obligations dressed as boilerplate (export control/ITAR/EAR, attorneys'-fee shifting, securities-trading acknowledgments, government transfer rights) that import compliance burden or financial exposure absent from Amperesand's standard. Notices/misc should be the cleanest part of the agreement; deviations here are signals of template drift or counterparty overreach rather than legitimate trade-offs.

walk_away_triggers: Bundled multiple Singapore-law statutory references embedded in a Delaware/US-governed agreement, creating governing-law conflict over personal-data definitions, related-corporation definitions, and signature validity — must be cleaned up before signing, not accepted as artifact.
Attorneys'-fee / prevailing-party fee-shifting clause not in Amperesand's standard, creating asymmetric or bilateral litigation cost exposure — resist or strike.
Incomplete or blank counterparty notice details (placeholder name/title/email fields) left in an executed agreement, undermining valid service of notices — never sign with placeholder notice fields.
Unilateral right to transfer the NDA and all received Confidential Information to a government agency without further consent — refuse or cabin with consent/notice.
Securities-trading / material-non-public-information acknowledgment imposing affirmative internal compliance and personnel-advisory obligations beyond an NDA's scope — push back as out-of-scope.

Export-control clause that conditions disclosure on prior government permits/authorizations or makes one party liable for the other's unauthorized export, rather than each party bearing its own compliance — resist the asymmetric/operationally burdensome form.

Jury-trial waiver or other US-litigation-specific boilerplate inserted into a Singapore-governed agreement where it is legally inapplicable and signals counterparty drafting control — strike as inapplicable.
Perpetual / unlimited-in-time survival of personal-data or other miscellaneous obligations — cap to a defined term.
